187.stem:
A university uses gas to heat its buildings. Over a period of 10 weekdays during winter, the gas used each day was measured in megawatts (MW) and the average outside temperature each day was recorded in degrees Celsius (°C).

Using $x$ as the average daily outside temperature and $y$ as the total daily gas usage, the equation of the least-squares regression line was found.

The equation of the regression line predicts that when the temperature is $0^\circ\text{C}$, the daily gas usage is 236 MW.

The ten temperatures measured were: $0^\circ, 0^\circ, 0^\circ, 2^\circ, 5^\circ, 7^\circ, 8^\circ, 9^\circ, 9^\circ, 10^\circ$.

The total gas usage for the ten weekdays was 1840 MW.

In any bivariate dataset, the least-squares regression line passes through the point $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$, where $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean of the $x$-values and $\bar{y}$ is the sample mean of the $y$-values.

figures.cap: blank grid: daily gas usage (MW) 160-240 against average daily outside temperature 0-10 °C

parts.latex:
Using the information provided, plot the point $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$ and the $y$-intercept of the least-squares regression line on the grid.

\exfigure{296_q18_1}
parts.note: Mean point and intercept of a least-squares regression line: bivariate data analysis (Standard), not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-12-S2-08

parts.latex: What is the equation of the regression line?
In the context of the dataset, identify ONE problem with using the regression line to predict gas usage when the average outside temperature is $23^\circ\text{C}$.
parts.note: Extrapolation limits of a regression line: bivariate data analysis (Standard), not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-12-S2-08

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}\bar{x}&=\dfrac{0+0+0+2+5+7+8+9+9+10}{10}\\&=5\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\bar{y}&=\dfrac{1840}{10}\\&=184\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ (\bar{x},\bar{y})=(5,184)$$
\exfigure{295_q18_1}
criteria: Calculates $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$, and plots this point on the grid, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Correctly plots both points on the graph

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Slope of regression line}&=\dfrac{184-236}{5}\\&=-10.4\end{aligned}$$
$$\text{Gas usage}=236-10.4\times\text{temperature}$$
i.e.
$$y = 236 - 10.4x$$
criteria: Finds the slope of the regression line, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: When temperature is $23^\circ\text{C}$, the regression equation provides a negative answer, which is not physically possible (negative gas usage).

meta.top_criterion_original: Identifies one problem with predicting using the regression line

252.stem:
The graph below is adapted from a diagram in the New York Times series “Planet Fate”. It shows how the local fast-food sales change as the country prospers.

The two variables in this scatterplot are the percentage change of gross domestic product (GDP) per capita (horizontal axis, $x$) and the percentage change in fast food sales from 2010 to 2015 (vertical axis, $y$).

\exfigure{408_q20_1}

Using the data provided, the least-squares regression line was found to pass through points $A\,(12,\,28.94)$ and $B\,(0,\,20.3)$. The correlation coefficient was calculated to be $r=0.53$.

figures.cap: scatterplot of change in fast food sales vs change in GDP per capita with regression line through A and B

parts.latex: Describe the strength and direction of the correlation between the change in GDP per capita and the change in fast food sales.
parts.note: Strength and direction of correlation: bivariate data analysis (Standard), not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-12-S2-08

parts.latex: Find the equation of the regression line.
Interpret the meaning of the gradient of the regression line, with reference to the context.
parts.note: Interpreting the gradient of a regression line: bivariate data analysis (Standard), not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-12-S2-08

solutions.latex: It is a moderate positive correlation.

$$\begin{aligned} m &= \dfrac{28.94 - 20.3}{12 - 0} \\ &= 0.72 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y = 0.72x + 20.3$$

solutions.latex: For each percent increase in GDP, there was a $0.72\%$ increase in fast food sales on average.

323.stem:
A class of 30 students sat an algebra test and a geometry test. The results were displayed in a scatterplot, and a line of best fit was drawn, as shown in the graph below.

\exfigure{642_q8_1}

figures.cap: scatterplot of Geometry test results (G) against Algebra test result (A) with line of best fit

parts.latex: Using the graph, find the equation of the line of best fit in terms of $G$ and $A$.
Adrian looked at the scatterplot and said: “Students who perform well in Algebra, also perform well in Geometry.” Is the statement true for all students, justify your answer.
parts.note: Bivariate data analysis (scatterplots, association) is not in the 2024 Advanced course · Standard: MST-12-S1-06

solutions.latex:
$$m = \dfrac{50 - 30}{80 - 40} = \dfrac{20}{40} = \dfrac{1}{2}$$
Equation of the line of best fit:
$$\begin{aligned} y - 30 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(x - 40) \\ 2y - 60 &= x - 40 \\ x - 2y + 20 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ G = \dfrac{1}{2}A + 10$$
criteria: Finds the gradient, $\dfrac{1}{2}$, or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
The statement is only true for some students, as there are students who got $95$ marks in the Algebra test and only $32$ marks in the Geometry test.

OR

Incorrect, as a few students got higher marks in the Algebra test but low marks in the Geometry test.

meta.top_criterion_original: Not true for all, with counterexample from graph

parts.latex: $\Delta ABC$ has vertices $A(-3,1)$, $B(5,-3)$ and $C(4,5)$. $D$ is the midpoint of $AB$. Show that $CD\perp AB$.

solutions.latex:
$A(-3,1)$, $B(5,-3)$

$\therefore\ AB$ has gradient $\dfrac{1-(-3)}{-3-5}=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ and midpoint $D(1,-1)$.

$C(4,5)$

$\therefore\ CD$ has gradient $\dfrac{5-(-1)}{4-1}=2$.

$\therefore\ m_{CD}\times m_{AB}=-1$

$\therefore\ CD\perp AB$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. correct procedure but with one error in coordinates or gradients
Some progress, e.g. finds coordinates of $D$ or finds gradient of $AB$

parts.latex: What is the gradient of a line perpendicular to the line $y=2x+1$?

solutions.latex:
Perpendicular lines have gradients with product $-1$. The given line has gradient $2$:
$$-\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2=-1$$
so the perpendicular gradient is $-\dfrac{1}{2}$.

parts.latex: Solve the equation $5-x=\dfrac{2x}{3}$.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} 5-x&=\dfrac{2x}{3}\\ 3(5-x)&=2x\\ 15-3x&=2x\\ 15&=5x\\ \therefore\ x&=3 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Incorrect solution but with one correct step, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: line through A and B with E on it, segment DC, dotted perpendicular from E to D; NOT DRAWN TO SCALE

parts.latex: Show that $AB\parallel DC$.
Show that the equation of $AB$ is $x-3y+13=0$.
Find the equation of $ED$.

solutions.latex:
Using $m=\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$:
$$m_{AB}=\dfrac{6-3}{5+4}=\dfrac{3}{9}=\dfrac{1}{3}$$
$$m_{CD}=\dfrac{-2+1}{0-3}=\dfrac{-1}{-3}=\dfrac{1}{3}$$
$\therefore m_{AB}=m_{CD}$, and lines with the same gradient are parallel, so $AB\parallel DC$.
criteria: Finds both gradients, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: A concluding statement is required for full marks.

solutions.latex:
Using the point-gradient form with $A(-4,\,3)$ and $m=\dfrac{1}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-3&=\dfrac{1}{3}(x+4)\\3y-9&=x+4\\x-3y+13&=0\end{aligned}$$
Or, using $B(5,\,6)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-6&=\dfrac{1}{3}(x-5)\\3y-18&=x-5\\x-3y+13&=0\end{aligned}$$

Since $ED\perp AB$, $m_{ED}\times m_{AB}=-1$:
$$m_{ED}=-\dfrac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}=-3$$
Using $D(0,\,-2)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y+2&=-3(x-0)\\3x+y+2&=0\end{aligned}$$
or $y=-3x-2$.

figures.cap: perpendicular lines through (0,3) and (0,2) cutting the x-axis at L and M, LM = 5 [diagram not to scale]

solutions.latex:
$L$ is where $y=ax+3$ meets the $x$-axis: $ax+3=0$, so $x=-\dfrac{3}{a}$.

$M$ is where $y=bx+2$ meets the $x$-axis: $bx+2=0$, so $x=-\dfrac{2}{b}$.
$$\begin{aligned}LM&=-\dfrac{2}{b}-\left(-\dfrac{3}{a}\right)\\&=-\dfrac{2}{b}+\dfrac{3}{a}\end{aligned}$$
$LM=5$, and the lines are perpendicular, so $ab=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{2}{b}+\dfrac{3}{a}&=5\\3b-2a&=5ab &&(\text{multiply by } ab)\\3b-2a&=-5 &&\ldots(1)\end{aligned}$$
$$a=-\dfrac{1}{b}\quad\ldots(2)$$
Substituting (2) into (1):
$$\begin{aligned}3b-2\left(-\dfrac{1}{b}\right)&=-5\\3b+\dfrac{2}{b}&=-5\\3b^2+5b+2&=0\\(b+1)(3b+2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$b=-1$ or $b=-\dfrac{2}{3}$, so
$$\begin{cases}a=1\\b=-1\end{cases}\text{ or }\begin{cases}a=\dfrac{3}{2}\\[6pt]b=-\dfrac{2}{3}\end{cases}$$
Since $a>1$, $a=\dfrac{3}{2}$ and $b=-\dfrac{2}{3}$:
$$a+b=\dfrac{3}{2}-\dfrac{2}{3}=\dfrac{5}{6}$$

parts.latex: Find the equation of the line through the midpoint of the interval from $A(3,2)$ to $B(-7,8)$ perpendicular to the line $\dfrac{x}{6}+\dfrac{y}{2}=1$.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Midpoint of }AB&=\left(\dfrac{3+(-7)}{2},\dfrac{2+8}{2}\right)\\&=(-2,5)\end{aligned}$$
Multiplying $\dfrac{x}{6}+\dfrac{y}{2}=1$ by 6:
$$\begin{aligned}x+3y&=6\\3y&=6-x\end{aligned}$$
so its gradient is $m=-\dfrac{1}{3}$.

Perpendicular lines have $m_1\times m_2=-1$:
$$m_\perp=3$$
Using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$ at $(-2,5)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-5&=3(x+2)\\y&=3x+11\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the midpoint $(-2,5)$ AND the perpendicular gradient $3$, or equivalent merit
Finds the midpoint $(-2,5)$ OR the gradient $-\dfrac{1}{3}$ of the given line, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve the inequation $4x-13\le 11x+15$.

solutions.latex:
Collecting the $x$ terms on the left:
$$\begin{aligned}4x-11x&\le 15+13\\-7x&\le 28\end{aligned}$$
Dividing by $-7$ reverses the inequality:
$$\begin{aligned}x&\ge\dfrac{28}{-7}\\x&\ge -4\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Reverses the inequality sign when dividing by a negative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Layton has a five-year old brother whose right foot is 13 cm in length.

He extends the line of best fit and notes that it predicts that a five-year old should have a foot length of approximately 17.5 cm.

Give TWO reasons why Layton is incorrect to assume from the bivariate data that his brother has smaller than normal feet for a five-year old.
parts.note: Bivariate data: extrapolation and correlation strength · Standard: MST-12-S1-06

solutions.latex:
Using $(12,22.5)$ and $(19,27.5)$:
$$\begin{aligned} m&=\dfrac{27.5-22.5}{19-12}\\ &=\dfrac{5}{7} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y-22.5&=\dfrac{5}{7}(x-12)\\ y-22.5&=\dfrac{5}{7}x-\dfrac{60}{7}\\ y&=\dfrac{5}{7}x+\dfrac{195}{14} \end{aligned}$$

Layton is extrapolating well outside the data set, as the students measured were aged from 12 to 18; this is always problematic as it assumes a linear relationship which may not be true.

The strength of the relationship between age and foot length is low (the correlation coefficient is close to 0), so even interpolating within the correct age range would be unreliable.
criteria: Gives one correct reason, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: "The length of the relationship" reads as "The strength of the relationship"; "closed to 0" as "close to 0".

parts.latex:
Consider the simultaneous equations.

$$\begin{aligned}2ax+y-5&=0\\x+3y-2a&=0\end{aligned}$$

If the equations have no real solutions, what is the value of $a$?

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} 2ax+y-5 &= 0 && (1) \\ x+3y-2a &= 0 && (2) \end{aligned}$$

Make $y$ the subject:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{From (1)}: \ y &= -2ax+5 \\ \text{From (2)}: \ y &= -\dfrac{1}{3}x+\dfrac{2}{3}a \end{aligned}$$

Both are straight lines. No real solutions means no point of intersection, so the lines are parallel and have equal gradients:

$$\begin{aligned} -2a &= -\dfrac{1}{3} \\ a &= \dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: correct answer with simplified fraction form
